name: Methimazole topical

lead: Methimazole (thiamazole) is a prescription drug that treats hyperthyroidism by blocking an enzyme the thyroid needs to make hormone. In hair-loss circles it comes up as a topical idea, a scalp application intended to support hair density.

The published literature is about oral use for thyroid disease. A PubMed search for topical methimazole and androgenetic alopecia returned no studies, and a reference article lists hair loss among oral methimazole's side effects.

paras: No standard regimen exists. When discussed, the idea is a compounded liquid applied to the scalp. Methimazole is a prescription medicine, so any use is a matter for a clinician.

Oral methimazole can cause itching, nausea, hair loss, and rarely low white blood cell counts, liver injury and vasculitis, and it is not recommended in the first trimester of pregnancy. How these relate to scalp application has not been studied.

chain: Compounded methimazole applied to the scalp
Proposed local effect on hair follicles
angle.text: The idea is to use a drug known for lowering thyroid hormone as a topical for hair. The mechanism for hair is not established in published trials.

lead: Methimazole, also called thiamazole, is a cyclic thiourea drug that lowers thyroid hormone production by inhibiting thyroperoxidase. It treats Graves disease and other causes of hyperthyroidism, and was approved in the US in 1950 as Tapazole.[1]

In hair communities it is mentioned as a topical option for scalp use. The appearance goal is thicker-looking hair. Published research on methimazole concerns oral treatment of thyroid disease,[1][2] and a PubMed search for topical methimazole in androgenetic alopecia returned no results at the time of writing.[3]

paras: Methimazole is used for Graves disease, toxic multinodular goiter, before thyroid surgery and in veterinary care for cats.[1] Reviews describe thionamides as typically inducing remission of Graves disease.[2]

Oral use is associated with itching, hair loss, nausea and muscle pain, and rarely with agranulocytosis, liver failure and vasculitis. It is not recommended in the first trimester, and it interacts with drugs such as warfarin and digoxin.[1]
Methimazole was first made in 1889. Edwin B. Astwood published work in 1949 showing it superior to earlier antithyroid drugs, and Eli Lilly marketed it as Tapazole.[1]

No studies found of topical methimazole for hair. Trials of the drug in Graves disease include a randomized comparison showing hyperthyroidism recurred in 56 percent of conventionally treated patients versus 17 percent of those on long-term therapy.[4]
